item.title: Leader Behaviours and their Perception across Organizational Levels
item.content:encoded:
Iris K. Gauglitz, University of Bamberg

Peter Harms, University of Alabama's Culverhouse College of Business

Urszula Lagowska, NEOMA Business School

Birgit Schyns, NEOMA Business School

Kimberley Breevaart, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Leadership research increasingly recognizes the importance of examining both leader behaviours and their interpretations across organizational levels. Rather than treating behaviour and perception as competing perspectives, this special issue seeks to integrate them and explore how different organizational actors understand and react to leader actions in complex, modern workplaces.

The issue addresses gaps in current understanding, including how leader behaviours and their perceptions vary outside the leader-follower dyad, discrepancies between leader intentions and follower interpretations, and the effectiveness of leadership development programs. Contributors are encouraged to employ multilevel analytical approaches and diverse methodologies to capture the complexity of leadership dynamics.

Research submissions are invited across multiple areas: theoretical development of multilevel leadership models, investigation of underlying processes and contextual factors affecting behaviour perception, examination of interactions between organizational actors, and methodological innovations in measuring leader behaviour and perceptual biases.

Appel publié par European Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical models proposing new or conceptually advanced configurations of leader behaviour and its perceptions, which consider the role of new working contexts in shaping leader behaviours and their perceptions
  • Multi-level conceptualizations of the impact of leader behaviour at multiple levels of organizations with a view to understand how and why perceptions across levels differ
  • Studies including models that explain why and under which conditions leader behaviour and its perceptions affect workplace outcomes, notably when leaders and others differ in their perceptions/(perceived) intentions or when behaviour is perceived as inconsistent or ambivalent
  • Research that investigates polarisation in follower perceptions—why perceptions of the same behaviour may diverge significantly
  • Studies looking at leader and follower behaviour and their interaction, such as how behaviours from one party trigger behavioural reactions of the other party and what that means for an effective collaboration
  • Studies considering the role of organisational hierarchy in how leaders behave and how their behaviour is perceived
  • Contributions considering interactions between personality traits (e.g., leader–follower trait congruence) in shaping behavioural expressions and perceptual accuracy; team outcomes of leader behaviour, for example, perception differences between team members and how this affects outcomes; and relative leader behaviour, that is, perceptions of how one follower is treated compared to others
  • Studies that develop and validate new measures of leader behaviour (e.g., behavioural indicators)
  • Studies that develop new measures that allow for the measurement of perceptual biases in leadership ratings and studies using advanced statistical approaches (e.g., polynomial regression analyses, multilevel modelling, pattern approaches)

item.title: Thirty Years of Affective Events Theory: New Directions in the Knowledge Era
item.content:encoded:
Rita Rueff-Lopes, Esade, Universitat Ramon Llull

Russell Cropanzano, Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado

José Navarro, Universitat de Barcelona

Ana Junça-Silva, ISCTE—Lisbon University Institute

This special issue revisits Affective Events Theory three decades after its original formulation, examining how it applies to contemporary work environments characterized by digitalization, datafication, and AI-mediated interactions. The issue seeks to extend AET's core propositions to explain how employees experience and respond to affective micro-events in modern organizational contexts, incorporating theoretical advancements and methodological innovations developed over the past 30 years.

The special issue welcomes original empirical research, theoretical contributions, and review articles that advance AET's boundaries across diverse contexts. Contributions should engage with emerging themes such as digital and hybrid work, multilevel dynamics of emotions, knowledge-intensive work environments, cross-cultural perspectives, and novel methodological approaches including experience sampling and emotion sensing technologies. Scholars are encouraged to challenge AET's assumptions, extend its mechanisms, and explore how affective processes operate within complex socio-technical work landscapes.

Appel publié par European Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Revisiting the structure and boundaries of AET in digital, hybrid, and AI-augmented work contexts
  • Temporal, multilevel, and dynamic modeling of affective events in teams and organizations
  • Affective events in knowledge-intensive work, professional services, and virtual collaboration
  • Cross-cultural and individual differences in affective experience
  • Methodological advances such as experience sampling, multimodal emotion sensing, and computational text or voice analysis
  • Links between affective events and creativity, performance, well-being, and sustainability
  • Integrations with adjacent theories including emotion regulation, relational energy, job crafting, and affective climate
